content: After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” {{v:2}} He said, “Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.” {{v:3}} Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey; and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son. He split the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and went to the place of which God had told him. {{v:4}} On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place far off. {{v:5}} Abraham said to his young men, “Stay here with the donkey. The boy and I will go over there. We will worship, and come back to you.” {{v:6}} Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. He took in his hand the fire and the knife. They both went together. {{v:7}} Isaac spoke to Abraham his father, and said, “My father?” He said, “Here I am, my son.” He said, “Here is the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” {{v:8}} Abraham said, “God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” So they both went together. {{v:9}} They came to the place which God had told him of. Abraham built the altar there, and laid the wood in order, bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar, on the wood. {{v:10}} Abraham stretched out his hand, and took the knife to kill his son. {{v:11}} The LORD’s angel called to him out of the sky, and said, “Abraham, Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” {{v:12}} He said, “Don’t lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.” {{v:13}} Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and saw that behind him was a ram caught in the thicket by his horns. Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering instead of his son. {{v:14}} Abraham called the name of that place “The LORD Will Provide”. As it is said to this day, “On the LORD’s mountain, it will be provided.” {{v:15}} The LORD’s angel called to Abraham a second time out of the sky, {{v:16}} and said, “‘I have sworn by myself,’ says the LORD, ‘because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son, {{v:17}} that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your offspring greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your offspring will possess the gate of his enemies. {{v:18}} All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring, because you have obeyed my voice.’” {{v:19}} So Abraham returned to his young men, and they rose up and went together to Beersheba. Abraham lived at Beersheba.

facets.text: God's command to sacrifice Isaac is explicitly a test (nissah) of Abraham, not a divine desire for human sacrifice. The test reveals and perfects Abraham's faith, drawing out an obedience that holds nothing back—not even the son of promise. The angel's declaration "now I know that you fear God" shows that the trial's purpose was to manifest and prove a fear of God expressed through unreserved surrender.
facets.question: Why would God command Abraham to sacrifice his own son?

facets.text: Abraham's obedience is heroic precisely because Isaac is the son of the promise, through whom God had sworn to make a great nation. To offer Isaac seems to contradict God's own word, yet Abraham obeys, trusting that God can keep his promise even through death. This is the summit of faith: believing God against every appearance, which is why Abraham is called the father of all who believe.
facets.question: How could Abraham trust God's promise while being asked to destroy the son who was that promise?

facets.text: Isaac carrying the wood for his own sacrifice up the mountain of Moriah is a profound type of Christ carrying his cross to Calvary. The beloved and only son, offered by the father, prefigures the Father's offering of the beloved Son. The tradition reads this scene as a shadow of the true sacrifice that God himself would provide.
facets.question: How does Isaac carrying the wood prefigure Christ and the cross?

facets.text: Abraham's words "God will provide himself the lamb" are fulfilled proximately by the ram caught in the thicket and ultimately by the Lamb of God. The place is named "The LORD Will Provide," pointing beyond the ram to the definitive provision on God's mountain. Christian tradition sees here the promise that God himself would furnish the true sacrificial victim in Christ.
facets.question: What does it mean that God himself will provide the lamb for the sacrifice?

facets.text: The ram caught in the thicket dies in Isaac's place, offered "instead of his son." This substitution shows that God accepts a victim in place of the one condemned, foreshadowing the logic of atonement in which one dies for another. The freed Isaac and the slain ram together anticipate the sacrifice by which humanity is spared.
facets.question: What is the significance of the ram being sacrificed in Isaac's place?

facets.text: Because Abraham did not withhold his only son, God swears an oath by himself to bless him, multiply his offspring, and bless all nations through his descendant. This divine oath, grounded in Abraham's obedience, establishes the covenant promise that culminates in Christ, through whom all nations are truly blessed. God's self-sworn word makes the promise irrevocable.
facets.question: Why does God swear an oath to bless all nations through Abraham's offspring?

facets.text: The repeated response "Here I am"—to God, to Isaac, and again to the angel—expresses Abraham's total availability and readiness before both God and his son. This posture of presence and self-offering models the disposition of the faithful servant who is wholly at God's disposal. It anticipates the perfect "Behold, I come to do your will" of the obedient Son.
facets.question: What does Abraham's repeated answer 'Here I am' reveal about faithful obedience?

facets.text: Abraham tells his young men, "We will worship, and come back to you," speaking of the sacrifice as an act of worship and expressing confidence that both he and Isaac will return. The tradition sees in this an implicit faith in God's power to raise the dead or otherwise preserve the promise. The whole episode frames sacrificial obedience as the deepest form of worship.
facets.question: Why did Abraham say he and Isaac would both return from the mountain?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Genesis 22 recounts the binding of Isaac (the Aqedah): God tests Abraham's faith by commanding the sacrifice of his beloved only son, Abraham obeys, God provides a substitute ram, and swears an irrevocable covenant blessing—read by tradition as a type of Christ's sacrifice.

[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The command is a test of faith, not a desire for human sacrifice; its purpose is to reveal and perfect Abraham's unreserved fear of God.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: Abraham's faith is supreme because he trusts God's promise even when asked to give up the son of promise, making him father of all believers.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: Isaac carrying the wood up Moriah prefigures Christ carrying the cross to Calvary; the beloved only son offered by the father shadows the Father offering the Son.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: \"God will provide himself the lamb\" and the place named \"The LORD Will Provide\" point beyond the ram to the Lamb of God provided in Christ.
[TYPOLOGICAL | inferential]: The ram slain \"instead of his son\" enacts substitution, foreshadowing the atonement in which one dies in place of another.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: Because Abraham did not withhold his only son, God swears by himself an irrevocable oath to bless all nations through Abraham's offspring, fulfilled in Christ.
[DEVOTIONAL | inferential]: Abraham's repeated \"Here I am\" models total availability and self-offering before God, anticipating the Son's obedient \"Behold, I come to do your will.\"
[DEVOTIONAL | traditional]: Abraham calls the sacrifice worship and says both will return, expressing implicit faith in God's power to preserve the promise even through death.
